claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its simple solid-solution state.
Enhanced dynamic recovery is the primary mechanism governing the alloy's low hardness and strength.
High atomic symmetry and low lattice friction allow dislocations to rearrange and annihilate before extensive dislocation networks form.
Dynamic recovery limits strain hardening in homogeneous solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi.
Conventional cooling of equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi yields a simple solid-solution state with a typical coarse-grained microstructure.
The conventionally cooled material has an overall homogeneous elemental distribution, apart from possible minor local fluctuations.
Severe plastic deformation or rapid solidification will refine the grain structure.
Dislocation substructure and grain-boundary density mediate dynamic recovery and influence dislocation storage.
The conventional alloy has a high degree of crystallographic symmetry and low lattice distortion.
High crystallographic symmetry and low lattice distortion reduce barriers to dislocation motion.
Reduced barriers to dislocation motion enhance dynamic recovery.
Rapid dislocation annihilation or rearrangement prevents sufficient dislocation accumulation to strengthen the material.
Grain refinement will impede dynamic recovery by increasing grain-boundary area and limiting dislocation mobility.
Fine-grained samples produced by severe plastic deformation or rapid solidification should have higher hardness than the coarse-grained baseline.
Fine-grained samples should have higher yield strength than the coarse-grained baseline.
Fine-grained samples should exhibit a more pronounced strain-hardening rate than the coarse-grained baseline.
Minor Ti-related segregation or precipitation could influence dislocation behavior and contribute to the mechanical response.
